title: Real-Time GPU Job Scheduling Latency Prediction in Multi-Cluster Kubernetes - Sujoy Dutta, Bloomberg

segments.text: Hello everyone, welcome to this talk.
I'm Sujay Data from Bloomberg. Um, today
I'm going to talk about an uh very
practical problem we ran into in our ML
platform, the GPU job scheduling latency
and how we predicted it.
So a quick introduction about me. I'm a
senior software engineer in Bloomberg. I
work on the infrastructure that powers
the ML workloads especially the uh GPU
heavy training jobs.
So here's the road map. We'll start with
a real user pain point and then we'll
dig into why our first solution didn't
work and then I'll show you the design
that we landed on and we'll also go over
some of the learning lessons and how it
is being used right now.
So consider this scenario. A user
submits a Py job at 10:30 a.m. and then
at 11 it is pending. They grab lunch and
they come back and it's still pending.
Finally, it gets scheduled at 2:30 p.m.
So the whole time they were having no
idea whether it is just about to start
or whether they could cancel it and
resubmit it. And in many cases they tend
to do that as well. Like they would be
impatient and they would be just
cancelling it and resubmitting the same
request with the same number of GPUs. So
that uncertaintity that's what the
experience we wanted to fix for our
users.
So users need ETAs to plan their runs
and their pipelines. So when users can't
predict the wait times, they tend to do
the irrational things. So they over
request the GPUs, they submit the
duplicate jobs. And for us as the
platform teams, we had no signal that
the queue was backing up until the
tickets started coming in. So the users
would file into our platform tickets
saying that, hey, my job is already
queued up for this amount of time. Is it
going to start now? what's the ETA etc.
So when we received the users tickets at
that point we were then reactive trying
to clear up if some old jobs will need
to be deleted or if this job needs to be
prioritized. So we were being reactive
instead of being proactive.
So before we talk about the latency
prediction um let's quickly take a look
at how the job actually gets scheduled
in our system. So a user submits a job
uh through Qflow. In this example, a
pytor job requesting let's say three
GPUs. So Qflow creates the underlying
Kubernetes resources. However, before
the request reaches the cluster, the
workload goes through the jobuler.
So we use Karmada for our multicluster
job scheduling and orchestration.
So the scheduleuler evaluates uh the
available clusters. So here in this
example, let's say cluster A and cluster
B are available in that tier. And this
job scheduler would be looking at the
GPU capacities. It will be looking at
the policies constraints and then it
decides for this incoming job what would
be the best fit cluster. So here in this
case if the job had requested three
GPUs, so cluster A tend to have four
GPUs available for the user's job. So
the job scheduler would uh go over all
of these constraint details and the GPU
capacities and then pick the cluster
array for the user's job.
So the availability of the GPU and the
time taken to schedule the job can
introduce that GPU job scheduling
latency.
So here was the core insight for us. We
already had the data. So every time a
training job a pytor job runs and
executes we capture its job execution
time the various timestamps and all the
metrics associated with that particular
job. So the first solution obvious
solution we came up with was running
some bad jobs to get this aggregated
data and compute the average as a bad
job maybe overnight and we would be
already be uh computing that GPU latency
but this was happening as a bad job. So
at the end of the day the computation of
average times was calculated
but when we looked at the real painful
weights the 60 minute 90minut delays
they weren't happening randomly so they
were happening during the spikes um the
GPU workloads tend to be quite bursty so
you can think of like if everyone is
trying to submit a job during morning
hours all the jobs are requesting x
amount of GPUs almost at the same time
so that's like a peak period for does
then the spike could happen again at
some other point in point of time in the
day. So uh the spikes do happen but if
we c if we compute just the average from
previous data the spikes tend to get
hidden because the average smooths it
out a little bit. So that's when we
realized that we didn't need more data
to solve this problem. uh we needed live
signal not yesterday's metrics but just
today's traffic even so like last one
hour or so so like I mentioned the daily
averages smooth out the exact spikes so
we need to be like more real time we
need to see what was happening in that
job scheduler within that last 1 hour or
so
uh for us the karmmada scheduleuler also
helps in making that live system state
decision making and not just the
historical summaries is
so another insight was um not all jobs
wait the same way. So a one GPU job can
fit in almost anywhere. So it could fit
in in cluster A B because almost all the
clusters have maybe one or two GPUs
left. So the one GPU job can find a slot
very quickly. However, a 8GPU job can it
needs a chunk of a node. So and a 64 GPU
job GPU node job can need multiple nodes
to become available at the same time. So
there is that difference like how a one
GPU job goes in it may find its own time
slot very quickly whereas a large
request can find some time. So if we
were to average and put one GPU request,
64 GPU requests together, average and
give out a single number out that would
make the prediction sort of meaningless
because like I was mentioning the one
GPU job might get a pessimistic ETA
because we are averaging it out with a
higher request whereas a 64GPU job might
get a very optimistic one. Both would be
incorrect for the users uh incoming job.
So what we did was um we bucketed them
we bucketed them into three tiers and
I'll talk a little bit more about it uh
in the next couple of slides also. So we
uh bucketed them into three tiers small,
medium and large and each bucket has its
own rolling average. So a small bucket
you can think of one GPU jobs tend to be
like a very quick job let's say a
fine-tuning job or small embedding task.
this would be requiring one GPU job and
they would go in much faster whereas uh
full training could require like
multiple GPUs. So we will be
categorizing anything that is larger
than 10 GPUs as a large buckets.
Everything else was categorized in
between in medium. So these tiers were
defined at the start of the uh whole
process. So these were defined by us and
we want we are working towards a system
where we want the buckets bucketing
happen dynamically and I'll talk about
it in in a bit. Uh for now like the
simple bucketing strategy into the three
tiers was uh effective for us to give a
more closer and almost uh correct
estimated GPU latency for our users.
So what do we actually measure? So once
we had the buckets uh we needed a clean
signal. So the clean signal comes from
the scheduling object. So once the job
scheduler receives the user's request,
it creates up the object and in that
object has lot of properties and uh the
main uh property that we were looking at
is two timestamps. So at the creation
time when when the job enters into the
system a time stamp created is assigned
to that particular uh scheduling object
and then there is uh another time stamp
which is the last transition timestamp.
So the last transition timestamp is when
we are actually trying to capture the
moment where the scheduleuler is moving
the job from pending to the schedule
state. That means the scheduleuler as it
was making a decision whether cluster A
or B has enough resources after a while
let's say one cluster let's say cluster
A got the resource opened up the
scheduleuler would move it from the
queue to the actual cluster for
execution and that transition time is
what we would capture in the last
transition time. So the difference
between those two time stamp is the
queueing latency and we track it per
bucket. Like I was mentioning a small
GPU job may have a different sort of
requirements and we shouldn't be
considering it in the same group as a
large GPU job. So we uh try to get that
particular queuing latency per bucket.
So the number or the signal that we
calculate as the delta is the signal we
care about and that's the raw GPU
latency for a for a particular job.
So to make our predictions real time
what we did was we kept a fixed size
bucket or you can think of like a fixed
size window um say last 100 latency
samples per bucket. So this is dynamic
and maintain a running sum. So the
maintaining of the running sum helped us
avoid recomputation of all the x amount
of jobs every time from the job store.
So let so when a new sample comes in if
the window is full what we do is we
subtract the oldest value from the sum
and drop it and when we add the new
value comes in we add it to the running
sum. So the average is then just divide
this running sum by the size of the
queue at that point and which is not
absolutely like 100% going to be
accurate but it averages out to be the
correct time for the particular latency
for that particular tier and bucket. So
this gives us that constant time update
that we need at the very instant user is
submitting job because we don't have
that luxury to go back and calculate the
batch compute at that point. Um and yeah
and just to be clear we are not removing
the job from the job scheduleuler. We
are only considering this part of it for
the rotating latency measurements. So
this is uh purely for the latency
prediction.
So this is the user experience delta. So
on the left side user were before
anxious constantly refreshing submitting
duplicate jobs requesting the same
amount of GPUs and wondering like if the
scheduleuler is broken why their job is
not getting submitted what is the delay
and after we started publishing this
latency value back to the user they they
were having more information okay so
let's say like the job is taking 14
minutes so they don't need to resubmit
it they can switch back to something
else or even 47 minutes or some another
number they can context switch to do
something else. But one thing to notice
is the underlying same infrastructure we
have the same Qflow supported cluster
but now it is communicating back to our
users. They are able to see what's
happening and how much time it may take
approximately. So we didn't eliminate
the weight but we eliminated the
uncertaintity and that predictability
changes the user behavior.
So one gotcha we hit at the very
beginning was what happens when the
controller which does all this
calculation in memory restarts. So the
rolling cues are currently in memory but
when the controller is restarting those
values are lost which means like the
first few prediction after the restart
has happened would be incorrect because
we would have no data in it. So we added
a hydration step to fix that. So on
startup um we query the internal job
data which I was mentioning earlier just
for the last hour of raw latency sample
and replay them into the rolling
windows. So it takes about only a very
few seconds but we have some data
representing the cluster status from
last 1 hour. So we m we try to maintain
the continuity and instead of giving a
value of zero seconds latency to our
users, we are able to still get the last
cluster state 1 hour ago and give them
some meaningful prediction.
Um so yeah so let's look into like how
we make this particular uh value
available to our users. So what we
actually publish is three main metrics.
So the first is the raw latency. So as I
was mentioning the delta between that
creating time stamp and the last
transition time stamp. So that is the
raw latency and this is our ground truth
for every single job. So it is useful
for tail analysis for us as a platform
team to see like how the jobs are doing
on the latency and set up some alerts on
our systems just in case if something is
going wrong but it is used mostly for
the tail analysis and the debugging
purposes.
Second, the rolling average. So this is
the important one, the rolling average
per bucket. And this is the ETA or
prediction signal we expose to our
users. So it reflects what's the average
GPU latency for their job in that
particular bucket in that tier.
And the third is the pending count. So
how many jobs are waiting right now to
get assigned a cluster. So these are
incoming jobs which are not which have
not found a cluster yet but the user has
already submitted a request for it but
they are all sitting and in a pending
state. So it will be useful for us as
platform team to know how backed up our
queue is. So we tend to keep this
information also in this particular
metric which is the pending count. So
all of these metrics feed into our
dashboards and other systems which can
consume from there and we also set
alerts when particular average latency
crosses a certain threshold so that we
know that the queue is backing up rather
than users reaching out to us first and
saying that hey where is my job I would
be able to tell them that okay we are
aware of it and they can do so and so to
remediate or submit their job sooner.
So let's zoom out and try to put uh put
it all together. So a user submits a
pytor job with the GPU request let's say
it enters the scheduleuler and the
eventually transitions from the pending
state to the running state or executing
state. So in our system uh the
controller which I was mentioning is
tracking the resource binding object. So
that is the scheduling object and the
controller watches it transition. So
when the exact moment of pending to
schedule happen we compute that queuing
latency.
So that latency sample is then pushed
into the rolling window for the
appropriate GPU bucket size and the
rolling average updates uh almost
instantly because of that constant time
calculation for that particular tier or
the bucket. So from there we have
finally the two outputs. The first one
is the publishing the matrix. So we
publish the raw latency, the average
latency and for ours we try to see the
number of pending jobs and then
eventually it is sent to the dashboards
and for alerting. The second thing we
publish is the at the submission time
what happens is users want to get a
response back immediately right like
they want to see what is the latency for
their job immediately at the time of
submission. So we try to give them that
approximate average latency which needs
to be accurate by using a web hook. The
web hook reads the current rolling
average from that particular cluster and
the tier and uh and it sees that okay
this is the approximate ETA because the
average calculated value is available
and so the user sees that estimate
immediately when they submit a new job
request. So it's a simple feedback loop
uh measure the present and then update
the signal and then expose it back to
our users in real time. So we avoid we
try to avoid doing any batch computation
at the time of job submission so that
there is no further delay and no
forecasting jobs are used. So it is
currently just event driven and updates
the uh job directly after the job is uh
submitted.
So what did we learn during this process
when we were implementing this solution?
So first exactly once processing. So uh
without careful predicates as I was
mentioning there is the time stamp the
last transition timestamp. So every
status update on that scheduling object
would introduce a new scheduling uh
value because uh sometimes an annotation
gets added or something else happened
the last transition timestamp could
change but we don't want to capture all
of those transitions. We want to capture
only once the transition and that is
from pending to the schedule. and we
make it happen using uh predicates.
Uh the second learning point for us is
the buckets over the precision. So yeah,
a general question could be like uh we
only have let's say 128 GPUs. So we
could just assign one inmemory queue for
the latency calculation for each GPU
right like GPU one. So all the jobs with
request one GPU can have a separate Q
two can have a separate queue etc. But
for us as the platform team that would
be a cardinality nightmare. Uh so we
decided that uh we have to like
summarize it or categorize them little
more efficiently. So on our side the
three buckets turned out to be uh
sufficiently relevant because we had
some analysis done on the past uh
submission behavior of our users of
various GPU jobs. So the small, medium
and large category sufficed. And the
third learning for us was the cold
starts which I was mentioning that the
at the time of a deployment or a crash
the in-memory cues could get wiped out.
So we learned this hard way um after a
deployment wiped out our in-memory
windows. So this was also a great uh
learning experience for us at the early
stages of implementing this solution.
So uh with this information where are we
going next? Um first we do want to come
to a smarter bucketing system rather
than redefining the buckets in a static
way as small, medium, large. We do want
to have like dynamic boundaries which
could uh shift a little bit on the real
uh job submission data. So if there was
like a two three GPU jobs also behaving
similar as a 1 GPU job in terms of
latency, we do want that boundary to be
little more dynamic. We we would like
ideally for the data to define its own
segmentation. Second, uh this is the
correlation for us as platform users.
When latency spikes, why does it happen?
What's the cause of the latency spike?
So, is it the workload pressure or is it
a draining cluster or could it be some
GPU health issues? Uh we want to
correlate that latency with the cluster
state and the health events.
And finally, the holy grail, the
recommendations. So not just like here's
your wait time. We do want to move to a
situ to a state where we are able to
recommend back the users what would be
the ideal state. So if you request let's
say five GPUs instead of eight, you will
start 20 minutes sooner and that's
actionable for the users not like a 20
minute wait time for you. So we want to
provide some actionable insights to our
users as well. So we are exploring our
current latency data. We have all the
events from the past, the job
submissions from the past and the
latency that we have predicted for our
users. So we are generating this
historical data set and along with some
job completion signals we will be able
we are building the predictive models
that incorporate all of these variables
and uh features. So we want to move from
the v visibility to the guidance state.
So yeah um so next time um you see
something pending you'll know like there
is a better way and with that I would
like to conclude and open up for
questions.
